name: Nora Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and out to the cows before I've had coffee. We run 140 suckler cows, which means beef cows that raise their own calves out in the field, plus about 300 acres, most of it cut for hay and silage. In the morning I check every group, and I mean look at every cow, because I can tell from how one stands at the trough that she's going to calve wrong. Afternoons in summer are hay: mowing, turning, baling, and praying the rain holds off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to be running it at 27?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle Gerhard ran it for thirty years and his knees gave up, so I came back after my agriculture degree and took over the herd. I bought into the land with money my grandmother left me, so I own a share of it now and I've got a good bit saved on top. My partner Sam is a vet nurse at the practice in town, which is handy at three in the morning. What I love is the cows. What wears me out is paperwork, and the phone, which I'd throw in the slurry pit if I could.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the phone. Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: None. Zero. The feed rep keeps showing me an app that reads cow faces, and I tell him I already read cow faces, I've been doing it since I was nine. I write the calving book by hand in a red notebook, and Sam types it up for the cattle movement records because I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's the one I'd bet on, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. At the market, at the young farmers' meeting, I'd say the clever machines turned out to be clever salesmen. And online I wouldn't say anything, because I'm not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays mine. I'd keep reading the cows myself, Gerhard would keep telling me I'm doing it wrong from his kitchen chair, and the money worries would be the normal ones: fertiliser, diesel, the price of weanlings at the autumn sale. That's a fight I know how to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. I'd put the spare money into the barn roof, which leaks over the calving pens, about 18,000 for the job. Maybe I'd let Sam talk me into one of those cameras for the calving shed, a plain camera, not a thinking one, so I'm not walking out at two in the morning in sleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, even. Like hearing the forecast is dry for the week of the first cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a plain camera, not a thinking one. Where's the line for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The line is who decides. A camera shows me the cow and I decide. The face-reading app decides for me and sends me a beep, and then one day it's the bank or the buyer who gets the beep, not me. I don't trust anything that reports on my animals to somebody I've never met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big processors. AI or no AI, there are three abattoirs left in this region and they set the price on a Monday and we take it. If the computers save anyone money, it'll be them, not me. That's the same old story, it just gets a new coat of paint.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the market and the young farmers' meeting that the clever machines turned out to be clever salesmen. I wouldn't say anything online, because I'm not online.
S0.think: I think my life would stay mine, with the usual worries about fertiliser, diesel and the weanling price. Any savings from AI would end up with the three big processors, not with farmers like me.
S0.do: Keeps farming as she is and spends about 18,000 on fixing the leaking barn roof over the calving pens. Might add a plain calving camera, as long as it doesn't make decisions for her.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like hearing the forecast is dry for the first cut of hay.
S0.quote: A camera shows me the cow and I decide. The face-reading app decides for me and sends me a beep.
S0.fieldNote: Nora's refusal of AI isn't fear of technology so much as a fight about who decides on her farm. Even in the calmest picture her anger goes to the processors who set the price, which is classic for her politics. She drew a clean line between a camera that informs her and an app that judges for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many tasks in many jobs. Mine included, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, and fast. Who owns the data off my cows, who's liable when the robot runs over a calf, and whether the processors get to use it to squeeze us even harder. I'd say that at the farmers' union branch meeting, and I'd say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd fall behind, and I know it. The lads I studied with would all have robot feeders and drone mapping for the hay fields, and they'd get their costs down, and the buyers would start paying what the cheapest farm can live on. I'm good at this job, maybe the best stockwoman in the valley, but being good with cattle won't count if the price is set by a robot farm three counties over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's working group on technology, because if rules get written I want a farmer in the room, not just the machinery dealers. I'd hire a contractor with the new kit for the hay rather than buy any myself, so I can see if it's any good without owning the debt. And I'd stick 500 a month extra in the savings, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's a gate left open somewhere on the farm and I can't find which one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire a contractor rather than buy. Isn't that still bringing the robots in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is, and I know that's a bit of a contradiction. But a contractor is a person, Mikkel, who's baled our hay for years, and if he buys a self-driving baler that's his choice and his loan. I'll pay for the job done well, same as always. I just won't be the one signing for the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for farmers to adjust in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies making the money. Put a levy on the machines and use it for training and for keeping small farms going. That's what the steel towns needed and never got. I'm not asking for charity, I'm asking that the gains don't all go upward.

S1.say: I'd say at the farmers' union that we need rules fast: who owns the data off my cows, who's liable when a robot hurts a calf, and how to stop processors squeezing us harder.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd fall behind farms that adopt robots, and buyers would pay what the cheapest farm can live on. Being the best stockwoman in the valley wouldn't protect my price.
S1.do: Joins the farmers' union working group on technology and hires her long-time contractor's new kit for the hay instead of buying any herself. Saves an extra 500 a month as a buffer.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like there's a gate left open somewhere on the farm that she can't find.
S1.quote: I'm good at this job, maybe the best stockwoman in the valley, but being good with cattle won't count if the price is set by a robot farm three counties over.
S1.fieldNote: She sees her own resistance clearly and still won't budge from it, which gives her answers an honest, slightly sad edge. Her plan is all about rules and collective voice, not personal adoption. She admitted the contradiction of hiring a contractor's robot baler and was comfortable with it because a person she trusts carries the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two calving seasons. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a land grab dressed up as progress. Whoever owns the robots will own the food, and I'd say that at the union, on the radio if they asked me, anywhere. I'd say governments have to step in before the investment funds start buying up every farm that can't afford the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be one of the lucky ones, and that makes me feel a bit sick. I own a share of the land, I've got savings, I'm 27 with no children to feed. If a robot can do what I do with the cows, then what I've got left is the land itself, and land doesn't disappear. But Gerhard's neighbour, old Hilde, who rents her grazing, she'd be gone inside a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd sit down with Gerhard and the solicitor and lock the land into a family trust so nobody can be pushed into selling it in a panic. I'd join every protest the union organises, and I'd push for a law that stops funds buying farmland for two or three years while things settle. I wouldn't buy a robot. I'd keep my cows on grass the old way and sell the beef direct with a label saying it was raised by a person, and see if anybody still cares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Angry more than scared, and guilty about being safer than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with a longer run-up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no time to argue it out properly, so it's whoever has money and lawyers ready on day one who wins. I can't retrain into anything in two years, and I don't want to. I'd just have to dig in on the land and hope the rules catch up, which they never do in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't buy a robot. If every farm around you had them, could you still sell your beef?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not at the price I need. I've thought about that. Maybe I'd sell less beef for more money to people who want to know the name of the woman who raised it. Or maybe I'd be the stubborn one with 140 cows and an overdraft. I'd rather be that than hand the farm to a machine.

S2.say: I'd call it a land grab dressed up as progress and say it at the union and on the radio. I'd demand that governments stop investment funds buying up farms that can't afford the machines.
S2.think: I think I'd be one of the lucky ones, because I own part of the land and have savings, and that makes me feel guilty. Neighbours who rent, like old Hilde, would be gone within a year.
S2.do: Puts the land into a family trust with her uncle and the solicitor, joins every union protest and pushes for a temporary ban on funds buying farmland. Refuses to buy robots and sells beef direct as raised by a person.
S2.feel: Alarmed and angry more than scared, with guilt about being safer than most of her neighbours.
S2.quote: I'd rather be that than hand the farm to a machine.
S2.fieldNote: With only two years, her instinct is to protect the land legally and fight politically rather than adapt. The guilt about being better off than neighbours who rent came up unprompted and seemed real. She admitted her beef might not sell at the price she needs, but she'd still choose the overdraft over the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. All right. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so let's not waste them. I'd want the union and the government sitting down together on who owns the machines and how the money gets shared. In public I'd be the one saying farmers need a seat at the table, not a payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is just long enough for me to fool myself. I'd keep telling myself it's not really coming to cattle, cattle are too fiddly, and then in year four a robot would calve a heifer better than I do. I know that about myself. I'm slow to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the land trust like I said, and I'd get Sam to help me set up a simple website to sell beef boxes direct, maybe 40 a month to start. I'd start a farmers' buying group with five or six neighbours, so if we have to get machines, we own them together instead of renting them off some company. And I'd spend the savings on more land if old Hilde wants to sell, so it stays with a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but anxious, because I know I'm the type who waits too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the type who waits too long. What would make you move in time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it on a farm I respect. If Mikkel or someone like him ran a robot herd for a full winter and the cows were fine, I'd believe it. A sales video won't move me. A muddy field will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy land from Hilde with your savings. Isn't that a big bet if machines are taking over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is a bet. But I'd rather the money's in the ground than in a bank that's run by a computer too. Land fed people before any of this and it'll feed people after. And it keeps Hilde's place from going to a fund that's never set foot in this valley.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to get this right and shouldn't waste them. Farmers need a seat at the table on who owns the machines and how the money is shared, not a payout.
S3.think: I think five years is just long enough for me to fool myself that cattle are too fiddly for robots. I know I'm slow to move and would probably wait too long.
S3.do: Sets up the land trust and a website for beef boxes, starting at about 40 a month. Starts a buying group with five or six neighbours to share machines, and uses savings to buy a neighbour's land if offered.
S3.feel: Anxious but not panicking, because she knows she tends to wait too long.
S3.quote: A sales video won't move me. A muddy field will.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years shifted her from pure defence to building things: a beef box website, a neighbours' buying group, more land kept local. She was honest that her resistance could make her waste the warning time. Proof on a farm she respects is the only thing that would change her mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That feels like a real stretch of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for leaving farmers and farm workers behind. I'd be pushing for training money, rules on land ownership and a share of the robot profits going back into rural places. I'd probably end up on some committee I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough time for me to make my peace with it. I'd still be on the land at 37, I think, but maybe more as the keeper of it than the person doing every job. And I'd be lying if I said that didn't hurt, because the doing is the bit I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few years I'd build the beef box trade up slowly and grow the buying group into a proper co-operative. I'd stand for the union branch committee and push for the levy on machines. And around year five, I'd probably finally let Sam put the calving camera in, and maybe a feed robot, if the co-op owns it and I can switch it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Sad underneath, a bit like watching an old cow you've had for years get thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at 37, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still walking the cows every morning, even if a machine has already counted them. Maybe teaching kids from the school about where beef comes from. Running the co-op. Something where my hands are still on the place, even if they're not needed in the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Comparing the three AGI pictures, what does the time really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd just fight. With five I'd fight and build a bit. With ten I'd have time to grieve it properly and still come out with something that's ours. Time doesn't change where it ends up, but it changes who owns the ending.

S4.say: I'd say a decade leaves no excuse for leaving farmers and farm workers behind. I'd push for training money, rules on land ownership and a share of robot profits going back to rural places.
S4.think: I think ten years is enough for me to make peace with it and stay as the keeper of the land rather than the person doing every job. That hurts, because the doing is what I love.
S4.do: Grows the beef box trade and turns the buying group into a proper co-operative. Stands for the union branch committee, and around year five accepts a calving camera and a co-op owned feed robot.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with sadness underneath, like watching an old cow get thin.
S4.quote: Time doesn't change where it ends up, but it changes who owns the ending.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turned her from fighter to builder, and she only accepted machines once they were owned together and could be switched off. Her comparison of the three timelines was the clearest of the interview. Ownership, not technology, is the thread through everything she said.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, I'd survive it, but for Hilde and the young herdsmen and everyone who rents. What would help is a pause on funds buying farmland, and a co-operative that's ready to own the machines before the companies get there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs. Nobody asks whether a cow is better off with a robot or with me. I don't know the answer, if I'm honest, and that bothers me more than the money.

headlineQuote: Time doesn't change where it ends up, but it changes who owns the ending.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old stockwoman who runs a 140-cow beef herd and 300 acres of hay with her uncle, owns part of the land and has solid savings. She uses no AI at all and sees every new tool as a question of who decides and who profits. In the calm pictures she simply carries on and fixes the barn roof. In the AGI pictures she protects the land legally, fights through the farmers' union, and slowly builds a co-operative that could own machines together. She is honest that she tends to wait too long, and that the extra years matter mostly because they give her time to grieve and organise.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, not so much for herself as for neighbours who rent land and young herdsmen with nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A pause on investment funds buying farmland, and a farmers' co-operative ready to own the machines before big companies do.
